name: Zane Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the back office at Hartley Motors, a car dealership on the ring road. I do the registration paperwork for new cars, book customers in for services, and file the finance agreements in the big grey cabinets. It's the same rhythm every day, and I like that. Saturdays are mad because that's when people buy cars.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you find hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The finance paperwork. There are a lot of boxes and if I miss one, Paula (the office manager) sends it back with a yellow sticky note. I'm not quick with new systems, I'll admit that. I still live with my parents, so I've saved about fourteen months of pay, and I'm in no hurry to change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never trusted it anyway. The dealership put in a chatbot for service bookings last spring, and half the customers still ring me because it booked them on a Sunday. I'd say that to the lads in the workshop and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even a little bit of AI is aimed at my desk. Service bookings are a third of my day at Hartley Motors (the car dealership where he works). A better chatbot means one back-office person might be enough. Paula would be the one deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd carry on. I'd keep taking the phone bookings and doing the paperwork the way I was taught. I'd keep saving, and I'd maybe ask my uncle Bruno about his tyre shop, just to know my options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine most days. A small nagging feeling when the chatbot gets a booking right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the other back-office person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kerry, she's been there nine years and she's quicker than me. If it came down to one of us, I know who stays. I don't hold it against anyone, that's just business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the chatbot yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't use any of that. I'd rather pick up the phone and talk to the customer, because then I know it's done right.

do: Keep taking **phone bookings** and doing paperwork the usual way.
Keep **saving** while living with my parents.
Ask uncle Bruno about his **tyre shop**, just in case.
feel: Fine most days, with a small **nagging feeling** when the chatbot works.
S0.quote: Service bookings are a third of my day at Hartley Motors (the car dealership where he works). A better chatbot means one back-office person might be enough.
fieldNote: He knows his **colleague Kerry** would be kept over him.

He refuses to use **AI tools** himself, preferring the phone.

steps.text: Keep taking service bookings by phone the usual way
Keep saving most of each payslip while living at home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go, firms will always cut costs. Maybe the government should help people retrain, but I wouldn't make a big noise. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the one who goes. The paperwork, the bookings, the finance forms, that's all thinking work on a screen, and I'm the slow one. Kerry would learn the new system and I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a bit and see how Paula plays it, because I don't want to jump for nothing. If they started cutting hours, I'd ask to move to the parts counter, where you hand over brake pads and talk to mechanics. And I'd save even harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not panicking, but it'd sit on my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the parts counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's half hands-on. You're in the stores, finding the right part, carrying boxes. A computer can order brake pads, but someone still has to find them on the shelf, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got fourteen months saved. Why wait rather than move now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because moving is a risk too. If I jump to another office, that office changes the same way. I'd rather sit tight where people know me.

think: My work is **screen work**, and I'm the **slow one**.

do: **Wait and see** how Paula handles the changes.
Ask to move to the **parts counter** if hours get cut.

fieldNote: He sees the **hands-on** parts counter as a safer corner of the same firm.
He'd rather **sit tight** than move, even with savings.
He accepts he's **first to go** without blaming anyone.

steps.text: Wait to see how Paula handles the new booking system
Ask to transfer to the parts counter if hours drop
Put an extra 100 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's mad, too fast, and someone should slow it down. I'd say it at the dinner table and maybe at the pub. I still wouldn't go on marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, my job's gone. Paperwork and bookings are exactly what it does. Even the parts counter, the ordering side goes in 2028 and the shelves go when the robots come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring uncle Bruno straight away and ask him to take me on at the tyre shop. Fitting tyres is hands-on, so it's got a few years left. I'd keep living at home and not touch the savings unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. My stomach drops just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning the AI tools now, with two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't see the point. In two years the tools don't need me. I'd rather learn something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say stay with us as long as you need. My dad would say he told me to do an apprenticeship at sixteen. My dad would be right, which is annoying.

say: Two years is too fast; someone should **slow it down**.
I'd say it at home and the pub, not on **marches**.
think: **Paperwork and bookings** are exactly what AGI does.
Even the parts counter goes: ordering in **2028**, shelves around **2031**.
do: Ring **uncle Bruno** straight away about tyre fitting work.
Keep **living at home** to protect savings.
feel: **Scared**, with my stomach dropping at the thought.
S2.quote: My dad would say he told me to do an apprenticeship at sixteen. My dad would be right, which is annoying.
fieldNote: He still won't learn AI, saying the tools **won't need him**.
Family is his **safety net**: his parents' home and his uncle's tyre shop.
He applies the **robot gap** sensibly to the parts counter.

steps.text: Ask uncle Bruno for a job fitting tyres
Stay living with parents and keep savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable, and companies should give people notice. I'd say firms and the government should both chip in for training. Calmly, like a normal person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably waste the first two years hoping AGI isn't true. That's what I'm like. I'd know Hartley Motors goes paperless in the end, but I'd keep turning up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd keep working and saving. Around year two or three, I'd start at Bruno's on Saturdays to learn tyres and wheel alignment. If it worked out, I'd move there full time by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. Like waiting for exam results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would push you to start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing Kerry or Paula lose hours. Once it's real at my own desk, I'd move. Until then I'd tell myself it's just talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens around 2034, when robots can fit tyres?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd be 35. Maybe I'd be running the shop with Bruno by then, and owning something is safer than working for someone. Or maybe not.

say: Five years is **tight but doable** if companies give **notice**.
Firms and government should both **chip in** for training.
think: I'd probably **waste two years** hoping it isn't true.
Hartley Motors goes **paperless** eventually, but I'd keep turning up.
do: Keep **working and saving** in year one.
Work **Saturdays** at Bruno's tyre shop from year two or three.
Move to the **tyre shop** full time by 2030 if it works.
S3.quote: I'd probably waste the first two years hoping AGI isn't true. That's what I'm like.
fieldNote: He knows his own **delay** pattern and says so.
His trigger to move is **seeing cuts** at his own desk.
Owning part of a **family shop** appears as a hope, not a plan.

steps.text: Keep working at Hartley Motors and saving in year one
Work Saturdays at Bruno's tyre shop from year two
Hold off big moves until colleagues lose hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fine, there's time, nobody needs to panic. Plenty of jobs change over ten years anyway. I'd shrug, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd relax too much. Ten years sounds like forever to me. I'd probably still be at Hartley Motors (the car dealership where he works) until AGI was obvious. I'd be 37 by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep saving, maybe buy a small flat with the savings so I'm not at my parents' forever. I'd help at Bruno's now and then. Proper changes I'd leave for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit guilty that I'm not doing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is buying a flat a good idea if your job ends around 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a fair point. But rent costs money too, and a flat is something solid. I'd buy small and pay it down fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would 'later' actually be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I see it coming, I suppose. Maybe five years in. I know that's how people get caught out.

Lots of jobs **change** over ten years anyway.

I'd stay at Hartley Motors until it was **obvious**.

fieldNote: A decade makes him **complacent**, and he knows it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time and I'm slow, so I'd be stuck. What would help is a proper apprenticeship for people my age, not just for sixteen-year-olds, with some pay while you learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how long people would wait before doing anything. For me it's too long, and I know it. A push from someone I trust would help more than any advert.

headlineQuote: I'd rather pick up the phone and talk to the customer, because then I know it's done right.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old** back-office junior at Hartley Motors, a car dealership, who lives with his parents.
He has about **fourteen months** saved and avoids AI tools completely.
He blames **no one**, seeing cost-cutting as just how business works.
His escape route is family: uncle Bruno's **tyre shop**, which is hands-on.
He knows he **waits too long**, and with ten years he'd relax too much.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, because he's slow to change and has **no time**.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships** for adults in their late twenties, not only for **teenagers**.
